newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Canberra sees no more labour reform.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Canberra sees no more labour reform.

text.p: Australian Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith said on Monday the government was not planning a second wave of labour reforms once the current changes were passed by parliament.
"We have a lot to do to bed down these reforms. There is no second wave in contemplation," Reith told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
"There's a lot yet to be done, which is consequential to these reforms, and that will certainly keep me busy enough."

Reith announced on Sunday that the government had secured passage of its Workplace Relations Bill through an agreement with the Australian Democrats under which 171 amendments will be made to the bill.
The government needs the support of the Democrats to get the bill through the upper house Senate, where it does not have a clear majority.
Other non-government senators have said they would oppose the reforms or have indicated concerns about the new laws.
Reith said he believed the government's reforms would help to bring about a cultural change in the Australian workplace.
They would also set up a clearer definition of when industrial action was lawful or unlawful, he said.
"The other changes to the (enterprise bargaining) agreement process will encourage a more co-operative, harmonious approach to workplace negotiations," he said.
"That also helps to, over time, substantiate our belief that this legislation will reduce the level of industrial action in Australia."
The number of Australian labour disputes fell to 43 in July from 52 in June, the Australian Bureau of Statistics said on October 18.
But the total number of working days lost as a result of industrial disputes rose three percent to 137,300 days in July from 133,400 days in June.
Reith also said the reforms were part of the government's economic improvement programme, aimed at paving the way for lower interest rates.

"Certainly, the steps that the government has taken to tighten fiscal policy, to cut government spending, to cut out waste -- all of those measures, I think, pave the way for a more benign monetary policy application by the Reserve Bank," he said.
The government expected the Senate to pass the labour reform bill in the next few weeks, allowing Australia's new industrial relations system to become operational on February 1 next year, he said.
Reith also repeated earlier statements that the government had maintained the "basic integrity" of its reforms, despite the agreed amendments with the Democrats.
Australia will move towards a more deregulated labour market under the reforms, with unions playing a less significant role in wage negotiations.
